cards.member_phrase: WHOLE
cards.prose: Joshua's roll opens east of Jordan with Sihon, his city, his rivers, the whole stretch he ruled. The psalm needs none of that. It sings his name in one line and gives the whole deed to Yahuah (the LORD), *for his mercy endureth for ever*. The same king stands in both: a border in the memorial, a mercy in the song.
cards.member_sentence: Sihon's fall sung by name as a deed of Yahuah's (the LORD's) mercy that endureth for ever.

cards.member_phrase: WHOLE
cards.prose: Joshua gives Sihon his own verse and his own borders. The psalm puts him in one breath with Og and *all the kingdoms of Canaan*, the two kings east of Jordan at the head of the whole land. What the memorial spreads over a chapter, the praise of Yashar'el (Israel) gathers into a single line, and the one who smote them is Yahuah (the LORD).
cards.member_sentence: Sihon and Og named together with all the kingdoms of Canaan, the heads of Joshua's roll in one line of praise.

cards.member_phrase: WHOLE
cards.prose: Joshua remembers Og as a king out of *the remnant of the giants*, holding Ashtaroth and Edrei. The psalm does not dwell on what he was. It names him and hands the victory to Yahuah (the LORD), *for his mercy endureth for ever*. The giant king is one more line in a song about mercy, and that is the whole of his memorial there.
cards.member_sentence: Og the giant king named in the psalm as a deed of Yahuah's (the LORD's) enduring mercy.

cards.member_phrase: hath given you this land to possess it: ye shall pass over armed before your brethren
cards.prose: Joshua writes that Moses gave the east country to Reuben, Gad and half Manasseh. Deuteronomy keeps Moses' own words at the giving: the land was the gift of Yahuah (the LORD) to possess, and the men who received it were to cross over armed ahead of their brethren until the rest of the house had theirs. The possession came with a duty to the whole of Yashar'el (Israel).
cards.member_sentence: Moses' command at the giving of the east country: the land is Yahuah's (the LORD's) gift, and the tribes who hold it fight for their brethren.

cards.member_phrase: WHOLE
cards.prose: Moses gave the east country *for a possession*, Joshua says. The psalm says who gave it and what it is: Yahuah (the LORD) *gave their land for an heritage*, and gave it for his mercy's sake. A possession is what men hold by the sword; an heritage is what a father leaves his children. The psalm calls the land the second thing.
cards.member_sentence: The land given for an heritage by Yahuah's (the LORD's) mercy, not held as a possession won by the sword.

cards.member_phrase: WHOLE
cards.prose: The three tribes east of Jordan took their portion from Moses' hand. The psalm names whose heritage it is in the end: *Yashar'el (Israel) his servant*, the whole house, not three tribes and not the men who fought for it. Yahuah (the LORD) gave it to the servant he chose, for his mercy's sake, and the song keeps the giving for ever.
cards.member_sentence: The heritage is Yashar'el's (Israel's), his servant, the whole house, given by mercy that endureth for ever.

cards.member_phrase: broughtest them into the land, concerning which thou hadst promised to their fathers
cards.prose: Joshua divides the west country among the tribes. The Levites, confessing generations later, say why there were tribes to divide it among: Yahuah (the LORD) multiplied the children as the stars and brought them into the land he had promised their fathers. Abraham's stars and Abraham's land meet in Joshua's chapter. The dividing is a promise being kept, not a conquest being counted.
cards.member_sentence: The children multiplied as the stars and brought into the land promised to their fathers: the dividing of Joshua 12 is the promise kept.

cards.member_phrase: thou subduedst before them the inhabitants of the land, the Canaanites, and gavest them into their hands, with their kings
cards.prose: Joshua's chapter says Joshua and the children of Yashar'el (Israel) smote the kings and Joshua gave the land. The Levites tell the same story to Yahuah (the LORD) himself with a different subject: *thou subduedst before them the inhabitants of the land*, and *gavest them into their hands, with their kings*. The man's name is on the chapter; the deed is the Father's.
cards.member_sentence: The Levites' confession gives the subduing of the kings and the giving of the land to Yahuah (the LORD), not to Joshua.

cards.member_phrase: WHOLE
cards.prose: Joshua gave the tribes their possession *according to their divisions*. The psalm has no surveyor's line in it, only the gift and the people: *an heritage unto Yashar'el (Israel) his people*. Joshua measured the land out; Yahuah (the LORD) gave it, and the psalm goes straight on to the giver: *Thy name, O Yahuah (LORD), endureth for ever* (Psalm 135:13). The memorial of the kings is his.
cards.member_sentence: The land given as an heritage unto Yashar'el (Israel) his people, and the psalm turns at once to the name of the giver.

cards.member_phrase: WHOLE
cards.prose: *All the kings thirty and one* is the sum of a chapter that gives every king one line and the word *one*. The psalm adds the same column differently: *To him which smote great kings*, and the reason under it, *for his mercy endureth for ever*. Thirty-one lines of a memorial become one line of praise, and the one who smote them is named.
cards.member_sentence: The great kings smitten, the closing tally of Joshua's roll sung as one line of Yahuah's (the LORD's) mercy.

cards.member_phrase: WHOLE
cards.prose: Joshua's tally stops at thirty and one. The psalm never counts; it says *great nations* and *mighty kings* and leaves the number to the book that kept it. The two belong together because they are one deed told twice, once as a record for the land and once as a song for the house, and in the song it is Yahuah (the LORD) who smote them.
cards.member_sentence: Great nations smitten and mighty kings slain: the psalm's uncounted line for Joshua's thirty and one.

cards.member_phrase: thou subduedst before them the inhabitants of the land, the Canaanites, and gavest them into their hands, with their kings
cards.prose: The kings of Joshua's list were not beaten by a stronger people. The Levites say it to Yahuah (the LORD) himself in their confession: *thou subduedst before them the inhabitants of the land*, and *gavest them into their hands, with their kings*. Thirty and one is the number of times he did it. The memorial counts; the confession says whom to thank.
cards.member_sentence: The Levites confess that Yahuah (the LORD) subdued the land and gave its kings into Yashar'el's (Israel's) hands: Joshua's thirty and one.

cards.member_phrase: WHOLE
cards.prose: John says every eye shall see him come with the clouds. Matthew tells how a coming can be seen by every eye: like lightning out of the east that shines to the west, the whole sky at once, nothing hidden in a corner. The verse before it warns, *Behold, he is in the desert; go not forth: behold, he is in the secret chambers; believe it not* (Matthew 24:26). A coming every eye sees is a coming no one has to be told about.
cards.member_sentence: The coming seen as lightning from east to west, the whole sky at once, so that every eye sees it.

cards.member_phrase: WHOLE
cards.prose: Yahusha (Jesus) told Nicodemus that no man had gone up to heaven but the Son of Adam who came down from it. The Revelation shows when that changes: after the reign and the little season the raised witnesses hear *Come up hither* and ascend in a cloud while their enemies look on. This is the going up of his people that Paul set after the rising of the dead, *caught up together with them in the clouds* (1 Thessalonians 4:17).
cards.member_sentence: No man had ascended to heaven but the Son of Adam who came down, until the witnesses are called up.

cards.member_phrase: Then also all men shall rise, some unto glory and some unto shame.
cards.prose: The seventh trumpet names *the time of the dead, that they should be judged*. Benjamin's testament sets that hour in an order. First the fathers: *then shall ye see Enoch, Noah, and Shem, and Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob, rising on the right hand in gladness* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 140:6). Only after them *all men shall rise, some unto glory and some unto shame*, and the judging begins. That last rising is what the trumpet calls the time of the dead.
cards.member_sentence: All men rise, some to glory and some to shame, and then the judging: the time of the dead the trumpet names.

cards.member_phrase: shall Abraham and Isaac and Jacob arise unto life
cards.prose: John sees the beheaded live and reign with Messiah (Christ) a thousand years. The testament of Yahudah (Judah) holds the same rising and sets it in order: Abraham, Isaac and Jacob *arise unto life*, and the twelve sons stand as *chiefs of the tribes*, Levi first and so all in order. The first resurrection raises the fathers and the faithful slain into a kingdom laid out by tribes, and they reign with him.
cards.member_sentence: The fathers arise unto life and the sons stand as chiefs of the tribes: the first resurrection set out in order.

cards.member_phrase: and after many days shall they be visited
cards.prose: Isaiah saw the host of the high ones gathered like prisoners into the pit and shut up in the prison, and he added the clause that keeps the prison from being their end: *after many days shall they be visited*. John gives the many days their measure. When the thousand years are expired Satan is loosed out of his prison for a little season, and his end comes after it, not in the chain.
cards.member_sentence: The host shut up in the prison and visited after many days: the prison has a term set to it.
cards.flag: Joined the dragon-bound thread (20:1-3), whose summary already carries Isaiah 24:22 and the loosing, rather than the Gog and Magog thread anchored on 20:7-8, whose subject is the muster of the nations. Move it if you read the card as about the muster.

cards.member_phrase: Then also all men shall rise, some unto glory and some unto shame.
cards.prose: John sees small and great standing before the opened books. Benjamin's testament names the same standing: *all men shall rise, some unto glory and some unto shame*, and after the rising the judging. The order is the same in both, the dead raised first and then judged out of what is written, and the two ends of it, glory and shame, are the two the opened books divide.
cards.member_sentence: All men rise to glory or to shame and then are judged: the standing of small and great before the opened books.

cards.member_phrase: from the land of the north, and from all the lands whither he had driven them
cards.prose: Paul asks what the receiving of the cast away house will be, and answers, life from the dead. Jeremiah had already described the receiving. The oath that once named the deliverance out of Egypt will be sworn instead by the one who brought the children of Yashar'el (Israel) *from the land of the north* and from every land he drove them to, back into the land given to their fathers. The receiving is a homecoming, and the house that was driven out is the house that comes back.
cards.member_sentence: The children brought back from the north and from every land they were driven to, into the land of their fathers.

cards.member_phrase: I will send for many fishers, saith Yahuah (LORD), and they shall fish them
cards.prose: The receiving Paul calls life from the dead has workmen. Jeremiah hears Yahuah (the LORD) promise fishers first, and after them hunters who search every mountain and hill and the holes of the rocks, so that none of the driven out is left unfound. Yahusha (Jesus) called his first disciples with the same word: *Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men* (Matthew 4:19). Paul, sent among the Gentiles who were his own scattered kin, is in that fishing.
cards.member_sentence: Fishers sent first and hunters after them, until the driven out are found in every hill and every hole of the rocks.

cards.member_phrase: Jerusalem shall be trodden down of the Gentiles, until the times of the Gentiles be fulfilled
cards.prose: Two sentences, two untils. Yahusha (Jesus) says Jerusalem is trodden down of the Gentiles *until the times of the Gentiles be fulfilled*; Paul says the blindness on Yashar'el (Israel) is in part and lasts *until the fulness of the Gentiles be come in*. Neither verse spells out who these Gentiles are. What both say is that the treading down and the blindness have a term set to them, and Paul's next words name what follows: *And so all Yashar'el (Israel) shall be saved* (Romans 11:26).
cards.member_sentence: Jerusalem trodden down of the Gentiles until their times are fulfilled: the same term as the blindness in part.

cards.member_phrase: stript of the garments of the flesh
cards.prose: Isaiah, carried up through the heavens, sees Enoch and all who were with him *stript of the garments of the flesh* and standing in *their garments of the upper world*, like angels in great glory. Paul's catching up is a going up of that kind: the living and the raised taken together *to meet the Lord in the air*, the flesh left behind and the glory put on. It comes after the reign; *the dead in Messiah (Christ) shall rise first* (1 Thessalonians 4:16) is an earlier hour.
cards.member_sentence: Enoch and those with him seen stript of the flesh and clothed in the garments of the upper world, like angels.

cards.member_phrase: WHOLE
cards.prose: Isaiah's *afterwards* is Paul's *Then*. The going up does not open the story; it closes it. After the reign and the little season the saints *turn themselves upward in their garments*, and *their body will be left in the world*: the flesh stays, the garment goes up. Paul says the same of the living who remain, *caught up together with them in the clouds*, and sets it after the dead have risen, not before.
cards.member_sentence: Afterwards they turn upward in their garments and the body is left in the world: the going up comes last.

cards.member_phrase: until the fulness of the Gentiles be come in
cards.prose: El Shaddai (God Almighty) promises Jacob at Bethel *a nation and a company of nations*. Jacob later says of Ephraim, *his seed shall become a multitude of nations* (Genesis 48:19), and the house of Joseph became that, scattered and grown up among the nations. Paul's *fulness of the Gentiles* is that company come in at last. Not nations added to the house from outside, but Jacob's own company of nations gathered home, and the blindness in part ending when they are.
cards.member_sentence: The blindness in part lasts until the fulness of the Gentiles, Jacob's company of nations, is come in.

cards.member_phrase: I will raise unto David a righteous Branch, and a King shall reign and prosper
cards.prose: Ezekiel's twig is cropped from the top of the high cedar, tender, and planted by Yahuah's (the LORD's) own hand on the mountain. Jeremiah names what grows from it: a *righteous Branch* raised unto David, *a King* who reigns and does judgment in the earth. Where Zedekiah's vine withered for a broken oath, the planted twig becomes the reigning king, and Jeremiah's next verse gives the fruit: *In his days Yahudah (Judah) shall be saved, and Yashar'el (Israel) shall dwell safely* (Jeremiah 23:6), both houses under the one Branch.
cards.member_sentence: The righteous Branch raised unto David, a King who reigns: what Ezekiel's planted twig grows into.

cards.member_phrase: WHOLE
cards.prose: Esdras is told the world goes back to *the old silence* for seven days, *so that no man shall remain*. Jeremiah was shown that silence from inside it: the earth *without form, and void*, the heavens dark, and two verses on, *I beheld, and, lo, there was no man* (Jeremiah 4:25). They are the words of the first day before the light, *the earth was without form, and void* (Genesis 1:2). The old silence is the earth back in its first stillness, before it gives up its sleepers.
cards.member_sentence: The earth without form and void and the heavens without light: the old silence as Jeremiah saw it.

cards.member_phrase: Except I shall see in his hands the print of the nails
cards.prose: Baruch is told the dead come back in the form they went down in, so the living may know them for the same people. Thomas asks for exactly that: he will believe the risen one is the crucified one when he sees *the print of the nails* and puts his hand into the side. The marks are how the same man is known. He is not doubting a resurrection; he is holding it to its rule, and Yahusha (Jesus) met him there: *behold my hands* (John 20:27).
cards.member_sentence: Thomas asks to see the print of the nails: the risen one known as the crucified one by the marks he kept.
